articles.title: A Kentucky landowner paid $800,000 in 1998 for two acres beside the Ohio River despite floodplain rules adopted a year earlier; after never seeking a floodplain variance, it lost its compensation appeal in 2026
articles.summary: Buying land for development can involve risks that are not immediately visible, particularly when local regulations restrict how a property can be used.
articles.body: Buying land for development can involve risks that are not immediately visible, particularly when local regulations restrict how a property can be used. A Kentucky landowner that purchased a two-acre tract along the Ohio River for $800,000 in 1998 has lost its appeal seeking compensation over floodplain restrictions that it claimed prevented the planned development. The dispute centred on floodplain regulations introduced by local authorities in 1997, which limited construction in certain areas considered vulnerable to flooding.In an opinion rendered on October 30, 2026, the Kentucky Court of Appeals affirmed a Jefferson Circuit Court decision granting summary judgment to Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government and the Metropolitan Sewer District. According to the court's ruling, available on Justia under Lampton Securities Partnership, LLP v. Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government, the landowner had not obtained a final decision from the relevant authorities about what could be built on the property. It had also failed to seek a variance, an administrative exception that could have allowed development despite the restrictions. The appellate court consequently concluded that the compensation claim was premature.A development plan approved before floodplain restrictionsThe dispute originated in the early 1990s, when the owners of a roughly four-acre property along the Ohio River received approval from the Metropolitan Sewer District for a condominium development. The project was planned in two phases, with the first covering approximately two acres and the second intended for the remaining two acres. While the first phase was completed, the second portion, which later became the subject of the legal dispute, remained undeveloped. An electrical equipment building was constructed on the tract, and utility lines were installed, but no condominiums were built there.In 1997, Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government introduced floodplain ordinances following catastrophic flooding. The regulations restricted most new construction within the conveyance zone, a designated section of the floodplain intended to accommodate the movement of floodwater. The two-acre tract was located within this zone.The ordinances, however, included exceptions. They allowed certain construction that had already begun before the regulations took effect to continue. They also permitted affected property owners to apply for specific variances through the Metropolitan Sewer District's Floodplain Board.Landowner purchased the property after restrictionsLampton Securities Partnership purchased the two-acre tract in 1998 for $800,000, a year after the floodplain regulations were introduced. The tract sat largely idle for years before the partnership placed it on the market around 2019. The marketing materials described the land as suitable for commercial development. However, Metropolitan Sewer District personnel learned about the sale, leading to a meeting between the district's legal counsel and representatives of Lampton.During the meeting, the district's counsel expressed the view that the floodplain ordinances prevented development on the property. Lampton subsequently argued that the restrictions had deprived it of all economically beneficial uses of the land. Rather than applying for a variance or attempting to begin the second phase of the previously approved condominium project, the partnership filed a reverse condemnation lawsuit against the Metro Government and the Metropolitan Sewer District in May 2020.Reverse condemnation, also known as inverse condemnation, allows a property owner to seek compensation when government regulations or actions effectively take private property without formally acquiring it. Lampton argued that the restrictions amounted to such a taking.Court says compensation claim was prematureIn July 2025, the Jefferson Circuit Court granted summary judgment in favour of the two government entities. The lower court cited Lampton's failure to exhaust administrative remedies and the timing of its complaint. The partnership appealed, but the Kentucky Court of Appeals found that the case could be dismissed on another ground: the claim was not ripe for judicial review.The appellate judges explained that a regulatory taking cannot be established until the relevant authorities have made a final decision about how a property can be used. Property owners must generally follow reasonable administrative procedures, including pursuing available variance procedures, before claiming that regulations have eliminated the property's economic value.In this case, Lampton had received no final decision from the Floodplain Board. The court also noted that an opinion expressed by a Metropolitan Sewer District staff member was not an official determination of the property's permitted uses. The court rejected Lampton's argument that seeking a variance would have been futile. The Floodplain Board had the authority to grant exceptions, and the record showed that it had approved variances for other property owners.Ruling leaves possibility of a future lawsuitThe Court of Appeals also found insufficient evidence to establish that the Floodplain Board would inevitably reject Lampton's application. The district's representative had testified that the decision rested with the board, not individual staff members, and that no similar condominium development variance had previously been requested. The judges therefore concluded that Lampton had filed its compensation lawsuit before obtaining a final administrative decision on the property's permitted uses. They affirmed the Jefferson Circuit Court's summary judgment in favour of Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government and the Metropolitan Sewer District.Importantly, the ruling did not determine whether the property could ultimately be developed or whether the floodplain regulations amounted to a taking. The appellate court clarified that Lampton could bring another compensation claim in the future if it obtained a final administrative decision and its claim otherwise met the legal requirements.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Indiana father lost his $350,000-a-year job after 26 years and moved to Virginia for work; an October 29 court upheld giving his ex-wife sole legal custody of their son and ordering him to pay $4,000 in legal fees
articles.summary: An Indiana father who lost his $350,000-a-year job after 26 years and moved to Virginia for new employment has lost his appeal against a court decision
articles.body: An Indiana father who lost his $350,000-a-year job after 26 years and moved to Virginia for new employment has lost his appeal against a court decision giving his former wife sole legal custody and primary physical custody of their son.Scotty G Nabors challenged the custody arrangement and an order requiring him to pay $4,000 towards his ex-wife's legal fees. However, the Indiana Court of Appeals upheld both decisions on Thursday, finding that the changes were supported by evidence and were in the child's best interests.Nabors and his former wife, Jill A Nabors, divorced in December 2024, according to the details mentioned in the ruling. At the time, both lived in Bartholomew County, Indiana, and agreed to share responsibility for their son, who was born in July 2014. Their arrangement allowed the child to spend alternating weeks with each parent.That arrangement became difficult to maintain after both parents decided to relocate in 2025. Scotty moved to Virginia after finding another job, while Jill moved to Fairmount, Indiana, to live closer to her family. The distance between their new homes meant the existing weekly custody arrangement was no longer practical.The dispute eventually reached the courts, with both parents seeking changes to custody. Scotty wanted his son to move with him to Virginia, while Jill argued that the child should remain in Indiana.How Scotty's job loss led him to VirginiaScotty had worked for Cummins for 26 years before losing his job in March 2025. At the time of his termination, he earned approximately $350,000 annually, excluding bonuses.The couple disagreed over why he had lost his job. Scotty claimed Jill had sent photographs to his employer that made it appear he was drinking at work. Jill maintained that his drinking had caused his dismissal.During court proceedings, Scotty acknowledged previously consuming 1.75 litres of Jack Daniel's whiskey every one to two weeks. However, he said his drinking had decreased and denied consuming alcohol while working.After receiving a severance package, Scotty initially remained in Indiana and searched for employment. Unable to find a comparable position, he accepted a job with American Woodmark Corporation in Virginia, earning approximately $280,000 annually without bonuses.He moved to Stephens City in August 2025 and purchased a four-bedroom house with his new wife. The property included a separate bedroom for his son, and Scotty told the court that the neighbourhood offered good schools and activities for children.Meanwhile, Jill had moved to Fairmount with her new husband, whom she married in February 2025.Child's schooling influenced the decisionFollowing her move, Jill enrolled her son at Park Elementary School without Scotty's consent. Court records showed that the child had adjusted well to the new school, made friends and received all A grades and one B-minus during his first semester.The child also enjoyed living at his mother's property and continued meeting a close friend from Columbus approximately once a month.Although Scotty believed his son's academic performance had declined, Jill disputed this. The trial court found that the child was doing well in his new surroundings and saw no reason to move him away from his school and friends.The court also examined the parents' strained relationship. Evidence showed that both had behaved poorly towards each other, sometimes in their son's presence.In one incident in May 2025, Scotty took the child out of school without informing Jill or the school. When Jill could not contact him, she requested a police welfare check. Scotty later acknowledged that failing to notify the school was his mistake.In March 2026, the trial court awarded Jill sole legal custody and primary physical custody, while allowing Scotty parenting time under a revised arrangement.Why appeals court upheld custody and legal feesScotty challenged the decision, arguing that the court had focused too heavily on his behaviour while giving insufficient attention to Jill's actions. He also raised concerns about her new husband's previous battery conviction and requested a more structured schedule for telephone and video contact with his son.The appeals court rejected his arguments, finding that the lower court had considered the child's relationships, schooling, living arrangements and the parents' inability to communicate respectfully.It also upheld the $4,000 legal-fee award. Scotty earned approximately $5,384 weekly, compared with Jill's $825, and the judges found that this income difference supported the order.The court therefore concluded that the custody changes were justified by the parents' relocation and the child's circumstances.You use AI every day. articles.title: Martha Stewart says she 'really screwed up' with Halloween homeless costume
articles.summary: The veteran lifestyle guru has deleted a photo of herself wearing torn clothes and dirt on her face.
articles.body:
Veteran lifestyle guru Martha Stewart has admitted she "really screwed up" by dressing as a homeless person for Halloween.

The 85-year-old US entrepreneur and personality has deleted a photo of herself wearing torn clothes and dirt on her face, holding a sign saying: "I am hungry help me!!"

She posted a statement on Sunday saying she was "distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention".

That was followed by a fuller apology. "It's hard to admit when you've really screwed up. My earlier statement didn't go far enough. I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry."

Stewart had captioned her original Instagram photo: "My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!"

The post received a swift and sharp backlash.

"This sartorial take on a homeless person is a lot. Insulting? Demeaning? Confusing? All of the above," PR expert Molly McPherson wrote .

One person wrote on social media: "Why in the hell would you even think about wearing that as a costume?"

Another said: "Why would she do that? Who did she think would find that funny? Billionaires?"

Arguably the original lifestyle influencer, Stewart started a catering business in the 1970s and rose to fame in the 1990s when she started her own magazine, Martha Stewart Living.

She later became a billionaire, albeit briefly, when her media empire Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia was floated on the stock market in 1999.

But in 2004 she was sentenced to five months in prison after she was found guilty on a number of charges related to an insider trading scandal.

She has since attempted to rebuild her brand, starring in her own reality television show, expanding her food products and teaming up with rapper and friend Snoop Dogg for a television series.

In 2015, she sold Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia for more than $350m (£220m).

articles.title: Inquiries continue after five stabbed at Chandler's Ford Halloween party
articles.summary: Three boys aged 16 and two aged 17 were taken to hospital with serious injuries on Saturday night.
articles.body:
Police are hunting for attackers who stabbed five teenage boys at a Halloween party in Hampshire.

Officers said an "unknown group" had gained entry to the party at a house in Park Road, Chandler's Ford, and the stabbings happened shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday. Three boys aged 16 and two aged 17 were all taken to hospital with serious injuries.

Barton Peveril said it believes two of those attacked are students at the sixth form college. In a statement, it said support was being offered and "our thoughts are with the victims and their families".

Hampshire Police wants to speak to anyone who was there or has footage, including doorbell camera footage, covering Park Road and the nearby area.

In an email sent to parents, the college on the outskirts of Eastleigh, said: "We are doing all we can to support our Barton Peveril Community at this time.

"Students can access support through their student progress advisors and the health and wellbeing team.

"Security is always present at both entrances of the college to ensure that only Barton Peveril College students have access to the campus."

The head teacher of Thornden School in Chandler's Ford confirmed former students had been injured in the incident.

In a statement, Caroline Lowing said: "We understand that some of our former students have sustained injuries and are receiving treatment and support. This news has been deeply upsetting for our school community.

"We are working to support any current students and families who may be affected and have appropriate wellbeing support available within school."

Eastleigh MP Liz Jarvis said: "The community is in just shock this morning that such an awful thing could have occurred.

"My thoughts are with the parents of the boys, the boys and the whole community.

"It is very sad to think that these five boys have been put in hospital as a result of this incident."

The MP urged people to "stay calm, don't be tempted to share misinformation online and let the police do their job".

Senior investigating officer Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie said they were trying to identify anyone who had been at the party, "whether that be having directly witnessed what took place, having filmed any footage which may be relevant, or who may be able to help us identify the unknown group."

Cordons have been placed along Park Road and Valley Road while officers speak to witnesses, check homes for video footage.

Police have also been speaking to residents at neighbouring houses and those in a number of other nearby streets.

Churches in Chandler's Ford are also opening open their doors to offer support. St Boniface and St Martin in the Wood said they would be available for people to pause for reflection or light a candle.

St Boniface Church in Hursley Road will be open 09:00-17:00 through the week, while St Martin in the Wood in Queen's Road will be available Monday and Wednesday between 15:00 and 17:00.

articles.title: South Korean lawmaker denied US visa for 1991 conviction. Three days later, he was issued A-2 visa after Marco Rubio's diplomatic intervention
articles.summary: A South Korean lawmaker who was initially denied a US visa over a decades-old criminal conviction was issued an official A-2 visa three days later,
articles.body: A South Korean lawmaker who was initially denied a US visa over a decades-old criminal conviction was issued an official A-2 visa three days later, following diplomatic intervention involving US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.Jin Sung-joon, chairman of South Korea's National Assembly National Defense Committee and a member of the ruling Democratic Party, received his visa from the US Embassy in Seoul on October 31, after his initial application was refused on October 28.The controversy centred on Jin's 1991 conviction under South Korea's National Security Act, for which he was sentenced to three years in prison and a three-year suspension of his civil rights. The exact reason for the initial visa refusal was not officially confirmed, although the lawmaker's past conviction was widely cited as a possible factor.Jin was seeking an A-2 visa, a category issued to foreign government officials travelling to the United States on official government business. He was scheduled to join a bipartisan South Korean parliamentary delegation visiting the US Indo-Pacific Command in Hawaii from November 1 to 5.What happened in the visa controversy?Jin announced the initial rejection on October 28 through a Facebook post, sharing what appeared to be a US visa refusal notice.He expressed strong regret over the decision, saying it was difficult to understand how the US could deny his application when he had previously visited the US Pacific Command in March 2014 as a member of a parliamentary committee.Jin said US authorities had requested court documents relating to his 1991 conviction, following which he submitted the relevant ruling.The case triggered diplomatic intervention from Seoul. South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul reportedly raised the matter with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth when the two met in the Philippines on October 28.South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun also raised the issue with Rubio on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta on October 30.On October 31, Rubio acknowledged the visa issue during a press conference in Atlanta, saying it appeared to involve an individual's actions from decades ago."I think there was one particular visa individually that there was an issue about regarding behavior perhaps a couple decades ago, but we'll work through that at a bilateral basis, not in a press conference," Rubio said.He indicated that the matter would be addressed through bilateral consultations between the two countries.Later that day, Jin announced that the US Embassy in Seoul had issued his A-2 visa, three days after the initial refusal."It is fortunate that the US State Department has issued the official A-2 visa, albeit belatedly," he said in his Facebook post.What was the South Korean lawmaker convicted of?Jin was convicted in 1991 of violating South Korea's National Security Act. He was sentenced to three years in prison and a three-year suspension of his qualifications.According to South Korean media reports, he was accused of organizing a group during his military service that spread anti-American and pro-North Korean views, including calls for the withdrawal of US troops from South Korea.He was pardoned and had his rights restored in 1995 as part of a special presidential pardon marking South Korea's Liberation Day.Jin has questioned why the decades-old conviction should affect his official visit, particularly given his previous visit to the US Pacific Command.The lawmaker departed for Hawaii on November 1 with a bipartisan delegation that included Democratic Party lawmakers Kim Byung-joo and Jin himself, along with People Power Party lawmaker Lim Jong-deuk and Reform Party lawmaker Chun Ha-ram. The delegation is scheduled to meet senior US military officials, including the commander of the US Pacific Command, to discuss bilateral security cooperation.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Virginia couple turned their gravel backyard into a garden for their toddlers after buying a century-old home; a year later, neighbour claimed part of the land was his and demanded that fence be removed
articles.summary: A Virginia couple who transformed the gravel backyard of their century-old home into a garden for their two toddlers have found themselves caught in a
articles.body: A Virginia couple who transformed the gravel backyard of their century-old home into a garden for their two toddlers have found themselves caught in a property-boundary dispute after a neighbouring property owner claimed part of the land belonged to him. Brittany Ellerbe and her husband bought the house in Petersburg in 2025 and turned the outdoor space into a garden with grass, flowers and vegetable beds. About a year later, the dispute escalated when workers arrived to remove part of their fence at the request of the neighbouring property's seller. The couple challenged the move in court, and a judge subsequently ordered that the fence could not be removed or relocated while the legal dispute continued.How a backyard makeover led to a disputeWhen Brittany Ellerbe and her husband bought their home on South Dunlop Street in Petersburg, Virginia, the backyard was largely covered in gravel. The couple gradually transformed it into a garden, adding grass, fencing and vegetable beds where they grew flowers, zucchini, squash and bush beans.The garden also gave the family, which includes two toddlers, a private outdoor space. But the transformation became the centre of a dispute about a year after they purchased the property.According to a report by local broadcaster 12 On Your Side, a realtor representing the seller of a neighbouring house on Wilcox Street told Ellerbe that part of the backyard, including an area near the couple's steps, belonged to his client. The realtor reportedly said part of the fence would have to be removed so the neighbouring property could be sold.Workers arrive to remove part of the fenceEllerbe told 12 On Your Side that the couple received no further communication for months before the seller arrived with a truck carrying workers who began removing part of the fence.The couple subsequently received a letter from an attorney and a land survey showing boundary lines. Part of the removed fencing was reportedly used to enclose another section of the neighbouring property.The incident prompted the couple to seek legal help. Ellerbe said they had not received a physical survey, a deed or a letter from an attorney before the fence was removed.The dispute centres on whether the contested section of the backyard legally belongs to the couple or the neighbouring property owner. The available reporting has not established that either side has conclusively proved its claim.A judge intervenes in the boundary disputeAfter hiring a lawyer, the couple obtained a court order in early October 2026. According to 12 On Your Side, a Petersburg judge granted an injunction and a temporary restraining order preventing the fence from being removed or moved until November 19, 2026.The order temporarily restricts further changes to the fence while the dispute proceeds. It does not constitute a final ruling on ownership of the disputed land.The case has raised questions about the property's historical records. Ellerbe told the broadcaster that the documents she had traced included an 1853 plat and a 1917 deed. She said she had struggled to find a recorded survey that clearly established the boundary.The judge reportedly raised concerns about missing records and whether the survey had been recorded. The underlying deeds, historic plats and survey would need to be examined to determine what they establish about the land.What the city and neighbouring owner have saidThe Petersburg assessor's office told 12 On Your Side that the matter appeared to be a legal dispute between property owners.The broadcaster also visited the neighbouring property and left contact information for the homeowner but reported that it had not received a response by the time its report was published.As a result, the publicly available account contains more detail from Ellerbe's side than from the neighbouring owner's perspective. The legal dispute remains focused on the property boundary and the evidence available to establish ownership.Why property surveys matter to homebuyersThe dispute highlights the importance of checking property boundaries when buying a home, particularly when fences, older deeds or historic land records are involved.Virginia's residential property disclosure guidance advises buyers to carry out their own due diligence because sellers do not make representations about current property lines. Buyers can seek information from local authorities and consider obtaining a property survey to help establish the boundaries of a parcel.A survey can provide important evidence, but a disagreement over ownership may also require examining deeds, historic plats and other legal records.You use AI every day. articles.title: Author Mitch Albom runs an orphanage for 56 children in gang-controlled Port-au-Prince; more than 50 teachers and staff continue caring for them behind its guarded walls
articles.summary: Mitch Albom’s orphanage in Haiti, Have Faith Haiti, shelters 56 children in gang-controlled Port-au-Prince, with more than 50 teachers and staff caring
articles.body: Mitch Albom’s orphanage in Haiti, Have Faith Haiti, shelters 56 children in gang-controlled Port-au-Prince, with more than 50 teachers and staff caring for them behind guarded walls. The bestselling author and his wife, Janine, take in abandoned infants, toddlers with disabilities and children begging in the streets. The city around them is a place where murder, rape and robbery are common, with hungry children standing just beyond the gate. The couple largely pay for the home themselves, and its stated mission is safety, nourishment, education and opportunity for impoverished children and orphans, plus stability for the staff and their families.How Mitch Albom helped repair a Haitian orphanage after the 2010 earthquake ended up running itThe earthquake of 2010 killed some 200,000 people and left more than a million homeless. Albom arrived in its aftermath and helped repair a Christian orphanage run by an elderly pastor, even though Albom himself is Jewish. The pastor, then 84, said he had no money to keep the place going. Albom told CBS News he blurted out an offer to run it himself, wondering how hard it could be.Janine Albom described the aim as giving the children a childhood, something that has been stolen from so many people outside the walls. Albom told the broadcaster that even a drop in the bucket matters if he and his wife can ease the hunger he sees beyond the gate.Helicopter flights, bulletproof convoys and a steel-doored bunker, the security behind the wallsInternational flights cannot safely land in the Haitian capital, so Albom flies every month to Cap-Haïtien. A helicopter run by a private security company then carries him to Port-au-Prince, where heavily armed guards drive him to the orphanage in a convoy of bulletproof vehicles.The journey reflects how far the country has fallen. Haiti’s government effectively collapsed in 2021 after the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse, and it has had no elected government since. Gangs now control as much as 90% of the area, and the United Nations estimates that more than a million people have been displaced by violence.From outside, the orphanage, with its 30-foot walls, barbed wire and guard towers, resembles a prison. Security is one of the biggest challenges for Yonel, the Haitian director. He runs surprise emergency drills in which the children grab “go bags” and hurry to a concrete bunker with steel doors. It holds a generator, a month’s supply of food and water, and cameras for watching the outside.Seven acres, no televisions and small classes, childhood spent inside the compoundMost of the children have not left the 7-acre compound in more than four years. They play, do chores, attend church and go to school without stepping outside. Lessons are taught in both French and English to prepare pupils for college, and classes are small. A child who struggles receives a customised lesson plan.There are no cellphones or televisions, and no computers for personal use. Albom told the broadcaster that this lets him see childhood in a purer form than in the United States, and that the children’s attention spans are remarkably long compared with those of American children.Not every child is an orphan, who is admitted, and the stories of those who grew up thereMany of the children were brought to the home by a desperate parent or relative who could not afford to feed them. Albom said the orphanage has to set conditions, because otherwise hundreds upon hundreds of children would arrive. It accepts a child only if there is one parent rather than two, if there is no proper home, or if illness is involved.The children’s stories show why. Bettinie, 17, arrived as a baby after her father died in the earthquake and her mother could not cope. Lorvens, also 17, came at three, malnourished. Gina was five when her father gave her up. She told CBS News that she “felt abandoned” and was frightened by the many new faces staring and smiling at her.Yonel understands that feeling. He was left at the original orphanage 36 years ago, aged five. Almost all the children now call him “father”, and he told the broadcaster that they need that connection, so he puts himself there for them.Sixteen graduates, scholarships abroad and a promise to come back and work unpaid for two yearsOver the past eight years, 16 pupils have finished high school at Have Faith Haiti, and every one received a scholarship to an American college or university. Each has also agreed to return and work at the orphanage for two years without pay. Albom said they are not going to America to take jobs but to seize an opportunity they cannot have at home, then come back and improve their country. Have Faith Haiti’s own website describes a pathway to college or vocational training for its graduates, who return home as changemakers and leaders.Sixteen Haitian college students spent their winter break in December 2025 at Albom’s home in Michigan. Bianka said she wants to bring education back to Haiti because leading a government or landing a good job requires it. Widley hopes to enter politics, though he acknowledges the turbulence and risk that come with it.Slow security deployment, cut American aid and uncertain visas cloud the next graduates’ futuresHaiti’s outlook remains unclear. In September 2025, the United Nations, with American backing, authorised a force of 5,500 international troops to support the overwhelmed Haitian police, yet fewer than 1,000 had been deployed. The United States has also reduced its financial obligations to Haiti by more than 50%.The uncertainty reaches the orphanage’s own students. Six were due to graduate that spring and would first spend a year volunteering in Haiti before applying for scholarships. Even with a scholarship in hand, a visa is not guaranteed. Albom remains hopeful, saying that children given something beautiful, calm and hopeful will aspire to those qualities.According to the Have Faith Haiti website, the orphanage is operated by A Hole in the Roof Foundation, a nonprofit founded by Albom, an author and journalist. In a message on the site, Albom writes that he has seen nowhere with greater despair, or greater hope, than Haiti.The website invites support in several ways: a monthly giving community called La Perle, one-off donations and volunteering. It also hosts Albom’s newsletter, “Life at the Orphanage”.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Government making up China policy as it goes along, say MPs
articles.summary: A report by the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee said decision-making had been characterised by "inconsistency".
articles.body:
The government has failed to deliver on its promise to pursue a consistent approach towards China and is instead making up policy "as it goes along", MPs on the business committee have said.

The committee said in its report that decision-making had been characterised by "inconsistency" and was heightening national security risks.

It called on ministers to block the transfer of sensitive data to China, give businesses clear rules for doing trade with the super power and ban imports made using forced labour.

The business department said it disagreed with the report's conclusion adding: "Our approach to China is consistent - we will co-operate where we can and challenge where we must."

"We have placed our relationship on a more stable, balanced, long-term footing, and based it on a clear-eyed assessment of both the opportunities and the risks.

"Our trade strategy makes clear that we will capitalise on every opportunity to grow our economy while never compromising on our national security, and our increased discussions with China allows us to directly raise concerns where they arise."

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer had sought to pursue a closer relationship with China, arguing that the UK could not afford to ignore economic opportunities, while insisting that should not mean compromising on national security.

However, efforts to build ties were criticised by some MPs concerned about China's alleged spying activities in the UK.

An audit of the two countries' relationship was carried out last year but the government has not published the document in full, saying it contained classified information.

Sir Keir's successor Andy Burnham has yet to set out his position on relations with China.

High Court upholds decision to allow Chinese mega embassy

China hits out at British Steel nationalisation

In its report, the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee said successive governments had "failed to reassure" the public they had taken "adequate measures to defend UK national security and economic resilience".

The MPs said the unpredictability of government approaches and a lack of clear guidance had hindered businesses ability to trade with China.

It proposed setting up "red" and "green" zones to clearly defining where trade and investment would be encouraged and the areas which were "off limits".

The committee said that the government should insist on fair trade with China and advised preparing tariffs that could be imposed if the country continued to subsidise its industry or failed to offer "fully reciprocal" market access.

On protecting sensitive technology and data, the report said there should be a ban on connected technology devices being used in critical national infrastructure.

The committee said "low-cost" Chinese connected technology had become wide-spread in the UK and that in this area the government had "prioritised diplomatic politeness over the UK's national security".

Universities should also get "faster advice" on conducting research with Chinese bodies, it said.

Committee chair and Labour MP Liam Byrne said: "Britain's businesses cannot plan for the future when the government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along.

"Ministers promised clarity and consistency. Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the eleventh hour.

"Britain must shape its own relationship with China, or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing."

articles.title: Two blue whale bones kept in London’s Natural History Museum reveal a 100-year-old link to South Georgia’s whaling industry and early efforts to regulate whale hunting
articles.summary: Two blue whale vertebrae kept at London’s Natural History Museum have helped uncover a century-old story linking the South Atlantic, a colonial exhibition
articles.body: Two blue whale vertebrae kept at London’s Natural History Museum have helped uncover a century-old story linking the South Atlantic, a colonial exhibition and efforts to regulate whaling. The bones were collected from the Falkland Islands Pavilion at the British Empire Exhibition in Wembley in November 1924. Their origins remained unclear for more than 100 years, until museum researcher Dr Sophia Nicolov traced their history through museum archive records.According to the Natural History Museum, the vertebrae came from one or two whales killed off South Georgia and were taken ashore for processing. The discovery also links the specimens to Sir Sidney Harmer, a former museum director who called for regulations as whale populations around South Georgia declined sharply.How did researchers connect the vertebrae to the 1924 British Empire ExhibitionThe investigation began when Dr Sophia Nicolov noticed discoloured labels attached to two large blue whale vertebrae in the museum’s cetacean collection. The handwritten notes identified the species as Balaenoptera musculus and recorded the date as 6 November 1924, with the Falkland Islands listed as the location.They also referred to the ‘Wembley Exhibition’, a name unfamiliar to Nicolov and Richard Sabin, the museum’s Principal Mammals Curator.Further research established that the reference meant the British Empire Exhibition, held at Wembley Park in 1924 and 1925. More than 27 million people visited the event, which presented the resources and industries of 56 dominions, colonies and protectorates represented across the British Empire.The Falkland Islands Pavilion showcased the whaling industryThe exhibition’s regional pavilions presented different aspects of the territories they represented. The Falkland Islands Pavilion also covered the Falkland Island Dependencies, including South Georgia and the South Shetlands.Whaling was the region’s largest industry, and the display included equipment used by the Southern Whaling and Sealing Company, owned by Lever Bros. Visitors could see harpoon guns, knives and hooks, alongside photographs showing how the tools were used.Whale products were then widely used in oils for machinery, soaps, margarine and other goods. The pavilion also displayed wildlife from the Southern Oceans, including whale remains. However, the two vertebrae were not visible in the archival photographs identified by Nicolov during her research.A century-old paper trail solved the whale bone mysteryNicolov found records in the museum’s archives confirming that the vertebrae had been displayed at Wembley. Letters showed that museum taxidermist Percy Stammwitz collected the bones from the Falkland Islands Pavilion on 5 November 1924. A separate letter from Sir Sidney Harmer to A. Radcliffe, manager of the Southern Whaling and Sealing Company, thanked him for the specimens.It stated that they came from either one or two whales killed off South Georgia and taken back to the island for processing. A memo from Harmer added that the vertebrae had remained on a beach in South Georgia for more than a year before they were collected and shipped to London for the exhibition.Why were the blue whale vertebrae important to Sir Sidney HarmerThe vertebrae were particularly relevant to Harmer, who had investigated the effects of whaling around South Georgia for more than a decade. Whale populations in the region had declined dramatically, and he was an early voice calling for regulations on the industry.Harmer later used the bones in a talk at the Zoological Society of London, although their role in research over the following century remains unclear. Nicolov and Sabin hope the improved information about the specimens' origins will make them more useful to scientists studying the effects of whaling.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Bristol's trees face growing pressure from disease and weather
articles.summary: The collapse of a 166-year-old copper beech raises concerns over Bristol's landmark trees.
articles.body:
Our oldest trees are increasingly vulnerable to disease, extreme weather and the effects of climate change.

The collapse of a 166-year-old copper beech in Bristol's Victoria Square, which was already scheduled for removal, has raised questions about the future of the city's landmark trees.

Scientists warn that there is additional pressure on mature trees, with damage to their roots potentially leaving them vulnerable to falling.

Professor Andy Bailey, an expert in molecular mycology, said: "Trees just can't change quickly to adapt to climate change."

Calls to remove liveable neighbourhood road

Live TV challenge for woman who overcame heartbreak

He said soil compaction, caused by people walking over root systems, can reduce the amount of air reaching roots and prevent water from draining properly.

Wetter winters can make the problem worse while hot, dry summers place additional stress on trees.

Fungal infections can then take hold, often developing over many years as they gradually destroy roots and undermine a tree's structural stability.

Professor Bailey said: "A combination of environmental pressures and natural ageing can make mature trees more susceptible to fungal infections."

However, not all fungi are harmful. Many are naturally present in British woodlands and play an important role in ecosystems, providing habitats for beetles and other organisms that depend on decaying wood.

Bristol-based naturalist Steve England said extreme weather was already affecting local ecosystems.

"Climate change is definitely affecting trees," he said.

"If you look at some of the berry-bearing trees like hawthorn or rowan, the berries are dehydrating really early."

He said this could leave migrating birds with less food, while prolonged rainfall can destabilise trees growing in heavy clay soils.

"When there's lots of rain it can impact areas with heavy clay soils as the water doesn't get the chance to drain away," he said.

He pointed to two large beech trees which have fallen in Stoke Park, explaining that saturated ground can leave their roots unable to withstand strong winds.

The loss of the Victoria Square copper beech has also resonated with residents.

For 77-year-old Frank, who lives near where the copper beech once stood, the trees have long been part of family folklore with his Scottish grandfather believing they brought bad luck and refusing to walk underneath them.

"He would tell me that hundreds of years ago in Germany, five brothers had a sword fight over a lady they all wished to marry," said Frank.

"This duel happened but they all tragically killed each other and their blood all pooled into a small hollow in the forest where there was a tiny beech sapling.

"As it grew its green leaves changed to red but its seeds became infertile. The only way for the beech to reproduce was by taking cuttings from it."

He added: "In time its origins have been forgotten but you still can't grow it from a seed!"

Bristol City Council confirmed the decision to remove the Victoria Square tree was made in September.

The council said its trees were inspected every one to five years, depending on how heavily the surrounding area was used.

A spokesperson said: "We use a range of measures to help protect and preserve significant trees, including regular inspections and soil management to support root systems."

Professor Bailey said that understanding the pressures facing mature trees, from fungal infections to changing weather patterns, would be key to protecting Bristol's landmark trees for future generations.

articles.title: As hundreds of polar bears prepare to gather near a Canadian town, conservationists are testing noisy drones to move them away from people, plus a camera warning system and electric fencing at a garbage site
articles.summary: Hundreds of polar bears are expected to gather near the Canadian town of Churchill in Manitoba as temperatures fall and the animals wait for Hudson Bay to
articles.body: Hundreds of polar bears are expected to gather near the Canadian town of Churchill in Manitoba as temperatures fall and the animals wait for Hudson Bay to freeze.To prevent dangerous encounters between the bears and local residents, conservationists are testing noisy drones that can guide the animals away from populated areas. They are also developing an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered warning system to detect approaching bears and installing electric fencing at a waste facility that attracts animals searching for food.The work is being carried out by Polar Bears International (PBI), a conservation organisation working to protect polar bears and Arctic sea ice, according to report by Global News.Churchill, often called the polar bear capital of the world, sees increased bear activity around this time every year. As temperatures drop, the animals move towards the coast and wait for sea ice to form. Once Hudson Bay freezes, they can return to the ice to hunt seals and other prey.However, climate change has made this annual movement more difficult. According to PBI, Hudson Bay now takes approximately one month longer to freeze than it did historically because of sea ice loss. This means polar bears spend more time on land, increasing the chances of coming into contact with people.Noisy drones help move polar bearsOne of the projects being tested in Churchill involves drones that use noise to encourage polar bears to move away from areas where they could encounter people.PBI is working with Brigham Young University (BYU) in Utah on the research. The team is examining whether drones can provide an affordable, non-lethal method of managing encounters between bears and humans.Kyle Garrett, a master's student at BYU who is working in Churchill, told Global News that the drone is slightly larger than an average model. Researchers fly it towards a bear, using the sound it produces to encourage the animal to move in a particular direction.If researchers want the bear to change direction, they adjust the drone's position. This allows them to guide its movement without physically approaching it.Garrett said the team's work so far suggests that drones can be effective in moving bears.AI-powered cameras to warn residents Another project focuses on detecting polar bears before they come too close to people. The system, called Bear-vision, is being tested at Churchill's waste facility. It combines radar and cameras to detect movement in the surrounding Arctic landscape and identify animals nearby.The technology is being developed to recognise polar bears and send alerts when one is detected. Data collected during the trials will help train the system to identify the animals and monitor their movements.PBI described the idea as similar to a home security camera, saying, "Imagine a doorbell camera that tells you if a polar bear is outside." Such warnings could help residents and workers avoid unexpected encounters with bears.The waste facility was selected because garbage can attract polar bears looking for food. According to Sky News, a fire in 2024 destroyed the site, which subsequently attracted bears searching for food.Electric fencing is also being installed at the facility as part of efforts to prevent the animals from entering dangerous areas.Beyond drones and cameras, researchers are testing other deterrents, including ultrasonic sound, conductive materials and a new odour-based bear spray formula.Climate change increasing encounters The conservation efforts come amid concerns about the long-term survival of polar bears in western Hudson Bay. According to PBI, the region's polar bear subpopulation has declined by almost half since 1979. The organisation links the decline to climate-driven sea ice loss and fewer female bears becoming pregnant.Sea ice is important because polar bears depend on it to hunt. When freezing is delayed, the animals must remain on land longer before returning to their hunting grounds.Geoff York, PBI's vice-president for science and policy, told Global News that falling temperatures signal to the bears that it is time to return towards the coast. This seasonal movement brings more animals into the Churchill area.The organisation is marking Polar Bear Week during the first seven days of November, coinciding with the annual gathering.Krista Wright, PBI's executive director, told Sky News that the organisation has worked with Churchill residents for decades to improve coexistence between humans and polar bears. "We're experiencing first-hand how co-existence is becoming part of everyday life in more places," she said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Bomb attack in western Colombia kills four, including baby, local official says
articles.summary: It is not yet clear who was behind the attack, which appears to have targeted a military base.
articles.body:
At least four people were killed when a lorry laden with explosives detonated in Tolima province, western Colombia, on Sunday, a local official has said.

A two-month-old baby girl was among the dead, Tolima governor Adriana Magali Matiz wrote in a post on X.

The lorry exploded near a military base in the town of Planadas, damaging a nearby hospital and several other buildings.

It is not yet clear who was behind the bombing, but armed criminal groups have recently stepped up attacks against the security forces in what appears to be retaliation for an offensive ordered against them by the new right-wing President, Abelardo de la Espriella.

Governor Matiz called the attack in Planadas "a vile and criminal act that we reject with absolute forcefulness".

"Attacking the civilian population and putting at risk the lives of our soldiers and the Tolima families is crossing a line that we will not tolerate," she added on X .

President de la Espriella, who campaigned on a tough-on-crime platform, wrote on social media that "we will not retreat, not even a millimetre".

Since he was sworn into office in August, the right-wing former defence lawyer has put an end to peace talks with some of Colombia's illegal armed groups, negotiations which had been started under his left-wing predecessor Gustavo Petro.

"In my government, criminals will have no political status, no leniency, and no impunity," de la Espriella wrote in a post on social media at the time .

At the start of his presidency, Petro had advocated for a "total peace strategy", arguing that only talks could lead to an end to the violence perpetrated by Colombia's many armed groups.

But after repeated breaches of the terms of the negotiations, Petro put some of the peace talks on hold.

De la Espriella has gone further, expanding his crackdown on all of the country's illegal groups, including bombing their camps.

These groups have in turn stepped up their attacks on the security forces, in some instances using drones - rather than cars or motorcycles - to transport the explosives.

In one of them, carried out on 23 October, a marine infantryman was killed and four others were injured aboard a Navy boat in Cauca province.

Writing on X after Sunday's bombing in Tolima, the president directly addressed what he said were "the narco-terrorists who continue to assassinate innocents".

"We're going to carry on with the bombings against legitimate military targets and we will step up our special operations," he stated, adding that those responsible would be "hunted down".

"This government will confront you, dismantle your organisations and restore security for Colombians."

articles.title: A Kansas burger stand began painting UFOs shaped like hamburgers on its wall in 2023, but city officials halted the mural as an oversized sign; on October 30, a federal appeals court ruled in the restaurant's favour
articles.summary: A historic burger restaurant in Kansas has won an important First Amendment victory after a federal appeals court ruled that city officials had no right
articles.body: A historic burger restaurant in Kansas has won an important First Amendment victory after a federal appeals court ruled that city officials had no right to stop it from painting hamburger-shaped flying saucers on its outside wall. On 30 October 2026, a three-judge panel of the 10th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in favour of Steve Howard, owner of the Cozy Inn in Salina, Kansas. The ruling supported an earlier decision by a lower court, which found that the City of Salina had violated Howard's constitutional rights by classifying his planned artwork as an illegal commercial sign. The dispute began in November 2023, when Howard hired local artist Colin Benson to paint a mural on the side of his building facing a public car park. The design showed UFOs shaped like hamburgers spraying ketchup and mustard. It also included the slogan, "Don't Fear the Smell! The Fun Is Inside!!". The painting work stopped suddenly after just six hours. City code enforcement officers told Benson to stop. Salina officials argued that the painting showed hamburgers and sauces sold inside the restaurant, making it an advertisement rather than public art. Under local rules, commercial signs have strict size limits, while non-commercial murals can be any size. Howard, with help from legal advocates at the Kansas Justice Institute, filed a federal lawsuit in February 2024 to protect his right to finish the artwork.Federal panel rejects traffic safety argumentsThe City of Salina defended its rules by saying that restrictions on commercial signs helped prevent driver distractions and protect pedestrians. However, the appeals court rejected these claims. It found that city officials had failed to show how a mural featuring hamburgers created a greater safety risk than a non-commercial painting that did not face the same restrictions. Writing the court's opinion, US Circuit Judge Scott Matheson Jr said the city had not provided enough evidence to explain why commercial artwork should be treated differently from other forms of public expression. During the case, the city submitted a student law review article, traffic presentation statistics, and evidence from city planner Dustin Herrs. During a deposition, Herrs was asked whether the city had scientific evidence showing that painted wall signs were more dangerous to pedestrians than painted murals. He did not confirm that such evidence existed. Salina also presented expert evidence from Mark White, a lawyer with a master's degree in regional planning. White referred to studies about how people respond to public art compared with commercial advertisements. However, Matheson noted in the court's opinion that White did not explain why the restaurant's planned artwork posed a greater threat to the city's interests than other displays that were allowed.Unlawful delay deemed a prior restraintAlong with rejecting the city's different treatment of commercial and non-commercial speech, the 10th Circuit panel also supported a lower court's finding that Salina had placed an unconstitutional restriction on free speech by failing to act on the permit application. After city officials stopped the artist from painting in 2023, Howard submitted an official sign permit application as instructed. However, city officials left the application waiting without making a final decision. "Given that Mr. Howard's application has aged for three years without his consent, Salina imposed a prior restraint on his speech," Matheson wrote in the panel's opinion. US Circuit Judge Gregory Phillips and US District Judge David Urias also joined the opinion. The legal fight began after Salina launched a wider effort to improve the appearance of its downtown area. In 2022, the city started holding an annual autumn mural festival. The event inspired Howard to add public artwork to his own building. "I was inspired," Howard said in an interview about how the project began. "I thought I was contributing to Salina downtown."Century of burger history in SalinaThe Cozy Inn is a well-known part of downtown Salina and has been operating from the same small shop, with just six stools, since 1922. The restaurant is famous for its small slider-style burgers, which are cooked with onions. Its tiny 40-square-foot customer area serves an average of 1,300 burgers each day. The menu is kept simple. Customers can order burgers, crisps, and canned drinks. Cheese is not available as an option. Howard, who started working in restaurants as a teenager, bought the historic business in 2007. Despite the two-year legal battle, Howard said he remained grateful for the support he had received from the local community. "Salina is my hometown; I love it here," Howard said in a statement released through the Kansas Justice Institute after the court ruling. "The reason I love this community, this town, is because of all of the support everyone has given me. Thank you for standing behind me and supporting me through this." Howard also said the national attention surrounding the legal case had unexpectedly helped the restaurant attract more customers. "My sales have gone up because people are coming to find out what the fuss is about," he said. "So thank you, city of Salina." Following the federal appeals court's decision, Howard plans to ask Benson to finish painting the flying saucer artwork on the restaurant's outside wall.You use AI every day. articles.title: Conservative Norfolk MP George Freeman fined for driving offence
articles.summary: The former Tory government transport minister says he "deeply regrets" his actions.
articles.body:
A former transport minister says he "deeply regrets" using a mobile phone while driving after he was fined and awarded six penalty points on his licence.

George Freeman, the Conservative MP for Mid Norfolk, pleaded guilty to the offence at Stratford Magistrates' Court in London on 1 September.

He was fined £430 and told to pay a surcharge of £172 to support justice services, as well as £130 in costs to the Metropolitan Police.

The MP said he was checking a navigation app while stuck in traffic.

Freeman, who served as transport minister under Boris Johnson between July 2019 and February 2020, said: "I was sitting in gridlocked traffic and checking Waze on my phone.

"I took full responsibility and deeply regret my actions."

He was seen checking his phone behind the wheel by a cyclist, who reported him to the police, the court heard.

The MP has spent 16 years in Parliament, having first being elected to represent Mid Norfolk in 2010, and held a number of ministerial positions when the Tories were in power.

The 59-year-old previously said he quit as science minister in 2023 because he could not afford rising mortgage repayments on a ministerial salary of nearly £120,000.

The move allowed him to make more money outside of government, in addition to the MP's salary at the time of £86,584, by taking on second jobs.

He became a paid adviser with GHGSat, a monitoring service for greenhouse gas emissions, in April 2024 and left the role in March 2025.

Last year, he was suspended from his role as a government trade envoy for Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore and Brunei after he referred himself to the parliamentary watchdog following claims that a GHGSat director helped him write questions to government departments.

The parliamentary watchdog considered the allegations and concluded that they did "not provide sufficient grounds" for a formal investigation.

articles.title: Poundland's former owner offers to invest in firm as minister prepares to meet board
articles.summary: Wolverhampton's Steve Smith says he attempted to contact Gordon Brothers but did not get a reply.
articles.body:
Poundland's former owner has said he would invest in the firm as a government minister said she would meet the firm's board.

Steve Smith, who left the Walsall-based business in 2006, said he had attempted to contact owners Gordon Brothers having been "really surprised" to learn about them filing for administration when sales were up 11% on last year.

The BBC understands that Business Minister Kate Dearden will meet with senior Poundland executives later this week to discuss the company's threatened insolvency.

US-based Gordon Brothers said it was evaluating interest for the whole business and formal and indicative offers for significant viable parts of it.

Gordon Brothers, who bought the firm from Polish retail group Pepco last year for £1, has stopped funding the business and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG).

The retailer has given the business until Thursday to find a rescue deal, putting up to 12,000 staff at risk.

It's understood the meeting with Deardon will be predominantly a "fact finding" meeting with government sources conceding there is limited scope for the government to intervene in a commercial transaction albeit one that puts over 10,000 jobs and hundreds of stores at risk.

The meeting was first reported by Sky News.

There is no current meeting planned between the government and executives from current owners, US private equity group Gordon Brothers.

Concerns have been raised that Gordon Brothers have declined an offer from another buyer to keep Poundland afloat in order to ensure repayment of £30 million loan it inherited after buying the company for £1.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government was "ready to support" staff as he also called for answers over why an offer to buy the business had been rejected.

Smith, from Wolverhampton and who set up the firm in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, said he contacted the owners over the last three months but had no reply. He had thought that was good news as he assumed the firm must have had offers on the table.

"And maybe I was a bit too late, but I'd certainly... with talking to the staff and how Poundland's performing at the moment, I'd certainly, if there's an opportunity, I definitely want to put some money back in there."

He said he was still in touch with staff there at levels within the business and "even last week" sales were 11.2 % upon last year.

"Although Poundland made a loss last year, they're going to make a good profit this year, so it's just crazy."

He warned that the two or three thousand suppliers to the firm only worked for Poundland so they would be directly affected by its collapse.

"This is not just about 12, 000 jobs. I'm estimating more like 20 or 30,000 jobs," he added.

The company has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and Smith said it had between four and five million customers a week, so with Poundland not being present on high streets would "cause a lot of other retailers to fall as well".

Liam Byrne, chair of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee and Labour MP for Birmingham Hodge Hill and Solihull North, said he felt the company could be saved and "the whole deal stinks to high heaven right now".

"Because I think the issue that we've got is, you've got an owner that could well be trying to cut and run, to sell a business that is in fact a going concern in order to maximize their own profits and put in jeopardy 12,000 British jobs on the high street."

"Our message today to government and to ministers is, do not leave this to the last minute, which is Thursday... please get on the case now to get everybody around the table to maximize every option to save as much of the business as possible," he added.

In a statement, the board of Poundland Limited said it had been "working on a formal sale process for Poundland" and despite "enormous efforts it had not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole".

"We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment."

Gordon Brothers said: "While Martin Property Group had been identified as the preferred bidder by Poundland's management team, attention must now turn to other active bids."

The interest, formal and indicative offers were being evaluated "with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland's people and all relevant stakeholders."

articles.title: Henry Nowak family say police failed them multiple times
articles.summary: The murdered student's family say they feel "manipulated" and "failed" by Hampshire Police.
articles.body:
The family of murdered student Henry Nowak have said police gave changing accounts of the events surrounding his death and did not initially disclose they had handcuffed him as he lay dying.

They said police initially portrayed him as the aggressor in the fatal altercation with killer Vickrum Digwa in Southampton on 3 December 2025.

The 18-year-old's stepmother Katie Nowak said Hampshire Police had failed them "multiple times".

The remarks came in a second excerpt released by ITV from the forthcoming documentary Dear Henry: Our Fight For Justice. Chief Constable Alexis Boon has apologised to the family and said that when Henry "needed us most, we failed him".

Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year student at the University of Southampton when he was murdered as he walked home from a night out.

He suffered five stab wounds or cuts from a 21cm (8in) blade, which Digwa later claimed was from a kirpan that he was carrying as part of his Sikh faith.

In police body-worn camera footage that was shown in court, the teenager could be heard repeating, "I've been stabbed", to which an officer replies: "Don't think you have, mate."

The family told ITV News they first saw the footage on the first day of Digwa's trial at Southampton Crown Court.

Henry's sister Olivia said: "That video only came out because there was a trial. We didn't see it before the trial."

Katie Nowak added: "We've always felt that there was a slight hope that Vickrum may have pleaded guilty.

"And if he'd have pleaded guilty or we hadn't have hired expert help, we've always had that fear that the truth may never have come out."

In another excerpt, she said: "I do feel that we have been failed multiple times.

"I fear that we may have been manipulated in our darkest hours.

"I fear that some decisions were made to try and protect the police and their reputation rather than help us as a family."

The teenager's father Mark Nowak said police gave differing accounts of what happened on 3 December.

"The story was evolving every time we had an interaction," he said.

"That evolution of what actually happened that night really shocked us, and we felt we were being hoodwinked. We felt we were being not told the truth."

He also recalled being asked to approve a draft police press release that depicted his son as an aggressor.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Chief Constable Alexis Boon told ITV in a statement: "Henry's murder was a devastating tragedy, and our thoughts remain with his family and all those who loved him.

"I am incredibly sorry that in his final moments, when he needed us most, we failed him.

"For Henry's family, this has been about more than the circumstances of one night.

"They have rightly raised serious concerns about the police response and their treatment throughout the investigation and since. No family should ever find themselves in this position."

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) confirmed its investigation into potential failures in the police response to Mr Nowak's stabbing is expected to be concluded early next year.

However, the family said they received a letter from the police watchdog in April, saying no officers would face a conduct or criminal investigation.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent inquiry into the murder , led by former lord chancellor Alex Chalk, which will look at "any missed opportunities to intervene".

articles.title: Driver who dragged cycling head teacher to his death gets life
articles.summary: Simon Richardson is told he will have to serve at least 25 years for the murder of Michael Mullins.
articles.body:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

A driver who dragged a head teacher to his death for more than a mile under the wheels of his car has been jailed for life for murder.

Simon Richardson, 35, crashed into 56-year-old Michael Mullins in Warburton, Greater Manchester, on 20 April as the married father-of-two cycled home from Stretford Grammar School in Trafford.

Jurors at Richardson's trial heard he then stopped to try to dislodge the injured but still-living cyclist before driving on with him still lodged underneath the vehicle.

The judge at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court told Richardson that he would have to serve a minimum of 25 years in prison.

Richardson had previous convictions for 28 offences, with a "significant history" of driving-related crimes.

He was also on bail at the time of the murder for offences including affray and assault occasioning actual bodily harm.

Mrs Justice Brenner KC said Richardson, who looked straight ahead as he was being sentenced, "took away a life and in doing so you caused devastation to a family and a community".

She added: "You deliberately used your car as a weapon over a prolonged period.

"You have repeated convictions for a range of serious driving offences over a 15-year period.

"This demonstrates the complete contempt you have for the law."

The judge told the court she had to hand Richardson a lifetime driving ban to "protect the public".

In her victim impact statement at the sentencing hearing, Mr Mullins' wife of 27 years, Sarah, said her husband had been her "safety net".

She spoke of the "all-consuming lethargy that makes it feel difficult to put one foot in front of another" since his death.

"My past, present and future have been brutally and callously torn apart, my present is empty and often seems to be without purpose," she said.

Elizabeth Baxter, acting head teacher at Stretford Grammar School, said it was an "honour and a privilege" to have worked alongside her predecessor.

Mr Mullins had led the school for 17 years before his death.

The court heard Richardson had an "appalling driving record" including previous convictions for drink driving and careless driving.

Judge Brenner said: "You heard [Mr Mullins] moaning for many minutes and I am sure you knew you were dragging a man who you believed was conscious for four-and-a-half minutes.

"You drove at speed, performed manoeuvres that would cause injury and even though you knew the state he was in, you carried on."

The court also heard it was "astonishing that no-one else was injured".

Referring to CCTV footage of the incident, Brenner said it was "too distressing to watch" as it captured an "astonishing disregard for human life".

"He could not have been more vulnerable," the judge added.

"You did that because you believe fleeing from the scene of the incident was more important than human life."

Richardson drove through "give-way" markings at a junction in Altrincham and into the path of father-of-two Mr Mullins, who fell on to his bonnet and windscreen before being drawn under the car.

Mr Mullins became entangled in the suspension of the 4×4 as Richardson drove on, the court heard.

Prosecutors said the defendant was aware the trapped cyclist was inches below his feet shortly after the collision in Paddock Lane, Warburton.

Richardson's front-seat passenger, his cousin Gabrielle Debotte, told the trial that both heard "moaning" from outside as he drove from the collision scene.

The prosecution said Richardson drove to a secluded farm track in Wet Gate Lane in Lymm, 1.3 miles (2.1km) from Paddock Lane, in a bid to dislodge Mr Mullins, who was "the single, solid piece of evidence of what he was driving away from".

He twice attempted to pull Mr Mullins out before returning to the car and veering sharply and deliberately from side to side before mounting a grass verge.

The court also heard Mr Mullins was finally released but Richardson reversed his vehicle over the head teacher and then drove away.

A motorcyclist later followed a trail of blood from Paddock Lane and discovered Mr Mullins lying alone and barely breathing on the grass verge, the court heard.

Emergency services were unable to save Mr Mullins, from Northwich, Cheshire, who died from multiple injuries.

Richardson was arrested the next day following a police chase

Defence barrister Jaime Hamilton KC said the absence of premeditation was a "significant feature" in the case, and that Richardson had not intended to use his vehicle as a weapon.

He was also convicted of dangerous driving in relation to the police pursuit on 21 April.

articles.title: Wizz Air flight from Luton in emergency landing after bomb threat
articles.summary: A Hungarian fighter jet escorted the aircraft to Budapest after the threat was received mid-air.
articles.body:
A Wizz Air flight travelling from London Luton Airport to Sofia has been escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet to Budapest after a mid-air bomb threat.

The aircraft was forced to make an emergency landing at Budapest Liszt Ferenc International.

Authorities there "carried out the necessary security checks on the aircraft and passengers", a spokesperson for Wizz Air said.

The airline later confirmed an inspection had been "completed and nothing was found", adding that the plane would depart again shortly. Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendis confirmed his country provided the fighter jet to escort the flight.

According to flight tracking website FlightAware, Wizz Air flight 4302 departed Luton at 08:33 GMT and was due to arrive in the Bulgarian capital at 13:25 local time (11:25 GMT).

But the website said it landed in Budapest at 12:09 local time (11:09 GMT).

In a post on social media, Ruszin-Szendis said that after receiving the bomb threat, the Wizz Air flight had requested permission to land at the airport in Budapest.

"Within minutes, a Hungarian Defence Forces Gripen fighter jet took to the skies and provided an escort for the passenger aircraft", he said.

After this, the jet returned to its base and police took charge of the incident, he added.

The airline said that after the plane made the emergency landing, it taxied "to a designated stand" where the security checks were carried out.

Wizz Air added that it was "cooperating fully with the authorities", and that the safety of passengers and crew "remains our highest priority".
