articles.title: A woman claimed she had received a Purple Heart and ran a foundation for homeless veterans; investigators found that she spent donations on a BMW and personal expenses
articles.summary: A New York woman who falsely claimed to have received a Purple Heart and used a veterans’ charity to solicit donations was sentenced to 12 months and one
articles.body: A New York woman who falsely claimed to have received a Purple Heart and used a veterans’ charity to solicit donations was sentenced to 12 months and one day in prison. Sharon Toney-Finch, 43, of Newburgh, had claimed that her foundation supported homeless and low-income veterans.She had founded the Yerik Israel Toney Foundation, a registered charity established in Sullivan County. She pleaded guilty in March 2025 to wire fraud and stolen valor offences.According to the US Department of Justice, she used donated money mainly for personal expenses, including a BMW, gym membership, travel and meals. The court also ordered her to serve three years of supervised release, pay $84,000 in restitution and forfeit $85,000.How did the foundation collect money in the name of veteransToney-Finch was an Army veteran who had been honourably discharged with various commendations. She founded the Yerik Israel Toney Foundation, a registered 501(c)(3) charity established in Sullivan County. The foundation reportedly aimed to raise awareness of premature births, assist premature babies and their families, and provide accommodation or transport while babies were in neonatal intensive care.It also claimed to help homeless and low-income military veterans who needed living assistance. However, prosecutors said the foundation was largely fraudulent. She provided little to no actual help to veterans, despite claiming that her foundation supported those in need. Instead, she used donations from other veterans’ charities to pay for her personal expenses. She obtained approximately $85,000 through the scheme, which included lying about her military service.Toney-Finch used charity donations to pay for her car and lifestyleThe money donated to the foundation was used principally for Toney-Finch’s personal benefit. The expenses included payments for her BMW, a gym membership, travel, meals and other personal costs. In June 2022, she persuaded a local foundation to give the YIT Foundation $10,000. The organisation provided grants to charities serving veterans, food pantries and domestic violence survivors.Toney-Finch said the money would fund the construction of housing for homeless veterans. Instead, she used the grant principally to pay for her luxury vehicle and personal expenses at bars, restaurants and gyms. The scheme involved approximately $85,000 in total, according to the case details released by federal prosecutors.What false claims did she make about her military serviceToney-Finch repeatedly presented herself as a military hero who had received a Purple Heart. She falsely claimed that she had been injured in an improvised explosive device attack in Iraq. She also altered her military discharge paperwork to make it appear that she had received the medal.In September 2021, she submitted a doctored military discharge certificate to the National Purple Heart Hall of Honor and was honoured at a Purple Heart ceremony alongside commissioned military officers.The following July, she appeared on a video podcast to discuss her foundation and military record. At the start of the appearance, she falsely described herself as a Purple Heart and Valor Award recipient although she never received a Purple Heart. She then recounted a fabricated attack and injuries requiring surgeries.A false story about homeless veterans led to a $25,000 donationIn May 2023, Toney-Finch made national news after telling a newspaper that her foundation had been supporting homeless veterans who were being evicted from a Newburgh hotel. She falsely claimed that the veterans were being forced out of the hotel to make room for migrants arriving by bus from New York City. At least one donor sent the foundation $25,000 after hearing the claims.Toney-Finch made false statements about housing homeless veterans who had supposedly been displaced by migrants. On September 30, 2025, she was sentenced by US District Judge Vincent L. Briccetti. The judge described her conduct as ‘appalling’ and ‘disrespectful to her fellow veterans’ when imposing the prison term.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available information, including records and statements released by the US Department of Justice. The Times of India has not independently verified the claims, financial transactions, or other details mentioned. articles.title: Learjet plane crash in Florida kills all 9 on board: What we know
articles.summary: The Learjet 60 went down near a road in Palm Beach County on Sunday. The cause is not yet known, and the NTSB has opened an investigation.
articles.body:
A private jet bound for the Bahamas crashed in Palm Beach County, Fla., Sunday afternoon, killing all nine people on board.

The Learjet 60, which had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, went down at about 12:50 p.m. ET near Cresthaven, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.

Dashcam footage posted to social media by an eyewitness showed the aircraft falling toward the ground beside a road and exploding into a fireball, narrowly missing cars and homes.

Duffy called the crash a "horrific tragedy" in a post on X , adding: "Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost."

Air traffic control audio posted on LiveATC captured the crew's comments leading up to the crash. Someone in the cockpit can be heard saying "Mayday, mayday," reporting the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute, Reuters reported. "We're going to crash into the ground," the person said.

The impact left a "massive crater" near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said at a news conference. About 600 residents were evacuated to two shelters, he said.

The National Transportation Safety Board has opened an investigation, and the cause is not yet known.

The Learjet 60 took off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. FAA records list the owner as a Delaware corporation.

The National Weather Service had a flood watch in effect for the area of the crash, Palm Beach County, through Monday afternoon, with rain expected on and off across South Florida.

In air traffic control audio posted on LiveATC, someone in the cockpit said they were "managing the ice" but faced "moderate" turbulence and were seeking "better rides." AP reported the crew also asked to climb.

Less than a minute later, the person said "Mayday, mayday," reporting the plane was suddenly descending at 10,000 feet per minute. Seconds later, the person declared an emergency, with the descent rate reaching 20,000 feet per minute.

Less than 20 seconds later, the person said: "We're going to crash into the ground," before reporting the descent rate had reached 22,000 feet per minute as the plane began to bank.

Flightradar24 data showed the vertical descent rate at one point exceeded 32,000 feet per minute. The last words heard from the cockpit were "we're out of time."

Accuweather reported that thunderstorms in the area produced heavy rainfall and lightning.

Driver Aki Kuusisto's dashcam footage captured the moment the jet hit the ground. "I heard a whistling noise, a big bang, and I saw a fireball," he told CBS News . "It felt like it was right next to us... you could feel it in the car."

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone injured on the ground.

Authorities haven't confirmed what caused the crash or identified the people on board. Steve Arroyo, an aviation safety expert, told the Associated Press that ice and turbulence could have caused the plane to stall.

The FAA said the aircraft departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was heading to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when the crash took place.

The FAA said it was investigating and would provide further updates.

DeSantis told reporters during a Sunday briefing that there were no reports of anyone on the ground being injured despite "a lot of debris" that was strewn over a "pretty significant distance."

"It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis said. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road."

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called the crash a "horrific tragedy" and said the FAA and Department of Transportation would be investigating the incident.

Anthony Blackmon, who lives around 500 feet from the site of the crash, told NBC Miami that debris from the crash struck his home.

"Debris was everywhere," he said. "Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire. I've always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today."

Adam Itayem told WPTV , "It sounded like a loud boom. I thought it was thunder," adding, "I saw a big crater in the ground and water coming out of the crater and a big fire too."

"I heard and felt the boom," Andrew Mannino told CNN , saying he saw a "large black cloud immerse in the air," adding, "The power immediately went out and is still out."

Around 600 people were evacuated by Palm Beach County authorities while federal officials investigate the crash.

"We're waiting for someone to give us answers about what we're going to do, because they're not even letting us into the community to get our clothes," local resident Jesus Solorzano told WPTV.
